landing.title: We All Breathe The Same Air · Sam Yazdanpanna
landing.waSubtitle: The new interactive graphic novel by Sam Yazdanpanna. What came after. How I became illegal.
landing.introLead: At seventeen, Sam had to leave Iran. Like Dust is the journey to Europe. We All Breathe The Same Air, his new graphic novel, is what came after.
landing.waReflectAlt: Grown-up Sam at an airport window sees his seventeen-year-old self reflected in the glass.
landing.waBody: A smuggler named Yilmaz, a fake passport, a plane to the Netherlands. Interrogations, a refugee camp, a wait that never seemed to end. Love, a little bird, and a letter that changed everything.
landing.waQuote: We all breathe the same air… but not all of us are equally free.
landing.ldTrailerAlt: Black-and-white drawing: a border officer studies a passport while young Sam waits.
landing.ldBody: Seventeen-year-old Sam travels from Iran to Europe, hoping to cross every kind of border. An interactive illustrated novel in black and white.

intro.youngAria: Click young Sam to begin the story
cues: My name is Sam.
I was born in Iran.
I was seventeen when I had to leave Iran.
My mother came with me as far as Istanbul…
…and then she went back to Iran.
There, a smuggler named Yilmaz handed me a fake passport…
…and put me on a plane.
Destination: the Netherlands.
And that's when it all began.
Interrogations… admission…
…and a wait that never seemed to end.
In the refugee camp, I fell in love.
I took care of a little bird.
And it was there that a letter reached me…
…one that changed everything.
When I turned eighteen, my life in Amsterdam began…
…undocumented and illegal.
This story is the story of what came before…
…how I became illegal.
We all breathe the same air…
…but not all of us are equally free.

1: Schiphol. The air was heavy with stories I didn't want to tell.
I was swallowed up and locked away. The walls whispered in a foreign language.
And then I saw that dog.
He looked at me as if he knew what secrets I carried with me.
“Passport please…” Welcome to freedom, I thought.
“Wait here please… Something's not right.”
But even freedom has guards.
Then the underbelly of Schiphol swallowed me.
Darker than my fear.
Time leaked away slowly.
I had never felt so alone.
“Where are you from?”
“How did you get here?”
“If you don't say anything, I can not help you…”
Hold on. No words, no mistakes. Every second of silence is a step further from being sent back.
After about an hour of saying nothing, they took me to a waiting room.
The Somali man searched my face for answers, but found none.
After what felt like an eternity, a guard with a dog appeared again.
They put us in a cold bus. My heart pounded in my throat.
Fuck! They're sending me back!
Planes roared overhead, their shadows warning of my fate.
Fuck!
Then the bus took an exit.
We're going somewhere else. But where?
“Take off your clothes!”
They searched everything and everywhere…
…then threw me into a cell.
I pulled on my clothes, wishing my dignity could be put back on just as easily.
What am I doing here?
Mother…
…I wish I was with you.
The next day they took me to a soulless building.
Every face was stern. Every voice brought another rule.
I was dropped off at the dormitory.
I had nothing but a $100 bill from my mother, hidden under my pillow as if it could keep me safe.
I tried to sleep, but every sound was danger and every shadow was a threat.
The few hours I slept…
“Wake up!”
That morning my old self got erased and I became a number in the system.
Then I got sent to something called the A… Z… C…
2: I was dropped off in front of a large building.
Was this what an AZC was?
After a brief introduction I was allowed to make a phone call.
For a moment, Mom's voice felt like home. Then the distance tore through me, and I swallowed the ache.
I was handed over to another guide. Who led me through a maze of hallways…
That night, all hell broke loose.
3: That morning I was summoned for an interview.
“Good morning.”
After a cold introduction, she noted inconsistencies in my story and asked for clarification.
What was I supposed to do? Lie? Tell the truth?
Where school was like a military academy.
Where every day began with a sermon about piety and religion.
Where even meeting up with a woman was forbidden.
Where my hair was cut whenever it grew long.
After writing down what I said, she said:
“We've opened a bank account for you. There's 500 guilders in it.”
“For a bike, clothes and school supplies.”
But I wasn't thinking about material stuff.
Amsterdam!
Taking in every little thing this city had to offer.
Remembering what freedom tasted like.
I didn't want to feel scared anymore.
It's been a long time since I've felt this light.
The city kept giving me reasons to forget.
The city kept nourishing me, mind and body.
I found my way into the city's veins,
moving with its rhythm, breathing in its life.
I found a wounded little creature, fragile and still.
Now, it was my turn to give something back.
4: From that day on, I finally started to feel a bit more at home.
I made friends. Both inside and outside the AZC.
I felt some freedom of movement in my life.
I tried to be cheerful, but that day I had received a letter from the IND.
The letter said I could still file an objection.
But I decided to leave the AZC.
To lose myself in the city and in illegality.
